questions.topic: Boundary-value pairing
questions.learningObjective: choose inputs that sit on a stated limit
questions.stem: A form accepts ages from 16 to 19. A team can afford only two boundary inputs. Which pair gives the most coverage?

15 and 20, the values just outside the range the form accepts
options.misconception: believes testing only the rejected side catches the same faults

options.text: 1 and 99, the smallest and largest ages a field could ever hold
options.misconception: believes extreme field values are the interesting boundaries

options.text: 17 and 18, the values sitting safely inside the accepted range
options.misconception: believes values inside the range test the range boundaries

6 is displayed, because the mean is rounded to the nearest whole

options.text: 4 is displayed, because the division is carried out before the sum is added

options.misconception: believes the helper computes a midpoint of pairs

2 is displayed, because only the two positive values were checked at all
options.misconception: believes a value that fails the first test is never checked again

options.text: 5 is displayed, because the negative value is checked once against each side

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Explaining why unreachable evidence is not evidence
questions.learningObjective: argue that a check outside the program's range proves nothing
questions.stem: A new check passes, and reading it shows it can only be reached if the routine returns a value the program never produces. Explain, in a short paragraph, why this passing check is not evidence that the change is correct.

answer.exemplar: A check can only report on behaviour it is in a position to reach, and this one is guarded behind a value the program never produces, so it would have passed before the change and passes now for the same reason. The guard means the check is measuring the guard, not the routine. What would make it evidence is either removing the unreachable condition so the check runs against real values, or adding a test that supplies a value the program can actually produce and comparing the two versions on it. A good answer therefore says the check is inert, explains why it is inert, and names the smallest change that would make it count.

questions.explanation: A strong answer says the check is unreachable, so it would have passed before the change as well and therefore distinguishes nothing, and it names a way to make it count. An answer that only says more testing is needed is too weak, because the point is that this particular testing cannot ever fail. The best answers also note that an inert check is worse than no check, since it occupies a line of the report and reassures the reader without having been asked a question.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to change for this check to fail.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Explaining the fate of a long-passing test
questions.learningObjective: argue that an unused check needs a decision rather than a habit
questions.stem: One check has passed every day for two years and nobody can name the fault it was written for. Explain, in a short paragraph, what a team should do about it and why leaving it alone is a decision too.

answer.exemplar: Leaving the check is a decision because it costs runtime, and it occupies a line in every report, so somebody should either establish what it protects or remove it. The investigation is cheap: read what it asserts, find the routine and the case it covers, and ask whether a change to that routine today would still be caught. If yes, the check earns its place and a comment should say which rule it protects. If no, deleting it frees runtime and removes a false signal. A good answer treats both outcomes as legitimate and rejects the habit of leaving checks in place because they have never complained.

questions.explanation: A strong answer treats the choice as a decision with a cost, and it names the cheap investigation that settles it: what does the check assert, and would it still fail if the routine it covers were broken today. An answer that simply says delete unused checks is too blunt, because some protect rules that a later change could break. The best answers note that a check nobody can explain is a check nobody will maintain when the routine it covers is rewritten.
questions.hint: Ask whether a change to that routine today would still be caught by it.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Explaining why a refactor lands alone
questions.learningObjective: argue for landing a structural change apart from a behaviour change
questions.stem: A developer has both tidied a routine and fixed a fault inside it. Explain, in a short paragraph, why landing them as two commits is better evidence than one commit doing both.

answer.exemplar: Two commits let the evidence be attached to the change that earned it. With the tidy landed first and green, the subsequent behaviour change sits on a known-good starting point, so if a check fails afterwards the failure belongs to the fix rather than to the reshaping. It also means the fix can be reverted on its own if it turns out to be wrong, which a mixed commit cannot offer. A good answer names both the attribution and the reversibility, and notes that a reviewer can skip the reshaping once it is green and spend attention on the fix.

questions.explanation: A strong answer names attribution and reversibility: with the reshaping landed first and green, a later failure belongs to the fix, and the fix can be undone without losing the tidying. An answer about tidiness or diff size is beside the point, since the point is what the evidence can be attached to. The best answers also note that a mixed commit forces a reviewer to check the reshaping properly, because if it is wrong the fix cannot be judged on its own.
questions.hint: Ask which change a later failure could be blamed on.
